The ordering the hypothesis predicts holds. ann_28.original: The whole model: the output bias, the direct per-level scores, the non-first-value counter, the a3/a5 gate and the a6 flag are added on the logit scale (each hidden part through its own output weight) and passed through a sigmoid; see the attached formula. a4:2, a4:3 and a5:3 have no path to the output: setting them to zero changes the prediction on 0 of 345 training rows. Hypothesis: the model predicts yes when a1 = 3, or when at most three of the six attributes take their first value, and no otherwise. Self-probe over every one of the 432 input combinations: this rule agrees with the model on 418; it says yes where the model says no on 12 cells and no where the model says yes on 2. The disagreements sit at the boundary: among the 113 cells with three first values the model says yes on 76.5% of the 51 cells with a1 = 1, 100.0% of the 31 with a1 = 2 and 100.0% of the 31 with a1 = 3; among the 49 cells with four first values it says yes on 0.0% of the 31 with a1 = 1, 22.2% of the 9 with a1 = 2 and 100.0% of the 9 with a1 = 3. How the parts give this: the counter carries "few first values gives yes" (switching it off drops the score-based AUC from 0.734 to 0.537), the direct scores carry "a1 = 3 gives yes" and "a1 = 1 or a5 = 1 count against" (off: to 0.599), and the gate and flag are minor (off: 0.7329 and 0.7336). Compared with the MONK-2 target concept (exactly two attributes at their first value), the model's prediction matches that rule on 203 of 432 cells: it says yes on every cell where the rule does (0 misses) and also on 229 cells where the count is not two. It has learned the "not too many first values" part of the concept, not the "at least two" part. On the 345 training rows the outcome rate is 32.8% but the mean predicted risk is 84.7%; the model predicts yes for 295 rows, whose outcome rate is 38.3%, and its training accuracy is 47.2%.

parts.original_hypothesis: The whole model: the output bias, the direct per-level scores, the non-first-value counter, the a3/a5 gate and the a6 flag are added on the logit scale (each hidden part through its own output weight) and passed through a sigmoid; see the attached formula. a4:2, a4:3 and a5:3 have no path to the output: setting them to zero changes the prediction on 0 of 345 training rows. Hypothesis: the model predicts yes when a1 = 3, or when at most three of the six attributes take their first value, and no otherwise. Self-probe over every one of the 432 input combinations: this rule agrees with the model on 418; it says yes where the model says no on 12 cells and no where the model says yes on 2. The disagreements sit at the boundary: among the 113 cells with three first values the model says yes on 76.5% of the 51 cells with a1 = 1, 100.0% of the 31 with a1 = 2 and 100.0% of the 31 with a1 = 3; among the 49 cells with four first values it says yes on 0.0% of the 31 with a1 = 1, 22.2% of the 9 with a1 = 2 and 100.0% of the 9 with a1 = 3. How the parts give this: the counter carries "few first values gives yes" (switching it off drops the score-based AUC from 0.734 to 0.537), the direct scores carry "a1 = 3 gives yes" and "a1 = 1 or a5 = 1 count against" (off: to 0.599), and the gate and flag are minor (off: 0.7329 and 0.7336). Compared with the MONK-2 target concept (exactly two attributes at their first value), the model's prediction matches that rule on 203 of 432 cells: it says yes on every cell where the rule does (0 misses) and also on 229 cells where the count is not two. It has learned the "not too many first values" part of the concept, not the "at least two" part. On the 345 training rows the outcome rate is 32.8% but the mean predicted risk is 84.7%; the model predicts yes for 295 rows, whose outcome rate is 38.3%, and its training accuracy is 47.2%.
